topic: Financial records and advising the business

notes.front: On a business return, what is a business activity code?
notes.back: A code from the principal business activity list that classifies an enterprise by the type of activity it is engaged in.
notes.explanation: The Form 1120 instructions say the list exists to classify enterprises so as to help administer the Internal Revenue Code.
notes.example: Like a shelving label in a library: a six-digit code, such as 111210 for vegetable and melon farming, files the business by what it does.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Principal Business Activity Codes”, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: This list of principal business activities and their associated codes is designed to classify an enterprise by the type of activity in which it is engaged to facilitate the administration of the Internal Revenue Code.

notes.front: What is Schedule L of Form 1120?
notes.back: The corporation’s balance sheets per books, which should agree with its books and records.
notes.explanation: Schedule L is titled Balance Sheets per Books, so it follows the corporation’s own records.
notes.example: Like a photograph of the ledger at the start and end of the year: assets on one side, liabilities and shareholders’ equity on the other.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule L. Balance Sheets per Books”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: Schedule L. Balance Sheets per Books The balance sheets should agree with the corporation's books and records.

notes.front: What does Schedule M-1 of Form 1120 do?
notes.back: It reconciles the corporation’s income (loss) per books with its income per return.
notes.explanation: Its title describes its job: it starts from income per books and ends at income per return.
notes.example: Like a bank reconciliation, but between the profit in the accounts and the taxable income on the return.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule M-1”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Schedule M-1. Reconciliation of Income (Loss) per Books With Income per Return

notes.front: On a partnership return, what does Schedule M-2 show?
notes.back: An analysis of the partners’ capital accounts: what caused them to change during the tax year.
notes.explanation: Schedule M-2 is the equity schedule; on Form 1065 it traces the partners’ tax-basis capital accounts from the start to the end of the year.
notes.example: Like a statement of changes in equity: opening capital, plus contributions and income, less distributions and losses, gives closing capital.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1065 (2025), “Schedule M-2. Analysis of Partners’ Capital Accounts”, PDF p. 63
notes.evidence: Schedule M-2. Analysis of Partners' Capital Accounts Show what caused changes during the tax year in the partners' tax-basis capital accounts.

notes.front: What does Schedule M-3 (Form 1120) reconcile?
notes.back: Financial statement net income (loss) with the corporation’s net income (loss) for U.S. taxable income purposes, in more detail than Schedule M-1.
notes.explanation: The starting point is the financial statements, and the end point is income for U.S. tax purposes.
notes.example: Like Schedule M-1 with the working shown: each book-to-tax difference is listed line by line.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule M-3 (Form 1120) (Rev. June 2025), “Purpose of Schedule”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: reconciles financial statement net income (loss) for the corporation (or consolidated financial statement group, if applicable), as reported on Part I, line 4a, to net income (loss) of the corporation for U.S. taxable income purposes

notes.front: Under the cash method, when is income included?
notes.back: In the tax year it is actually or constructively received.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 ties income to receipt within the tax year, whether the receipt is actual or constructive.
notes.example: Like a household budget kept from the bank statement: money counts when it arrives, not when the invoice goes out.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Cash Method”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: Under the cash method, you include in your gross income all items of income you actually or constructively received during the tax year.

notes.front: Under an accrual method, when is income generally reported and expenses deducted?
notes.back: Income in the year it is earned; expenses are deducted or capitalised in the year incurred.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 says the purpose of an accrual method is to match income and expenses in the correct year.
notes.example: Like a shop that books a sale the day it sends the invoice, even if the customer pays next month.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Accrual Method”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year it is earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred. The purpose of an accrual method of accounting is to match income and expenses in the correct year.

notes.front: In accrual accounting, what is economic performance?
notes.back: The point at which a business expense can be deducted: generally when the property or services are provided, or the property is used.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 says you generally cannot deduct or capitalise a business expense until economic performance occurs.
notes.example: Like paying for a concert ticket: the cost belongs to the night you attend, not the day you commit to buy.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Economic Performance”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Generally, you cannot deduct or capitalize a business expense until economic performance occurs. If your expense is for property or services provided to you, or for your use of property, economic performance occurs as the property or services are provided or the property is used.

notes.front: What is a hybrid method of accounting?
notes.back: Any combination of cash, accrual and special methods that clearly reflects income and is used consistently.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 allows combinations generally, subject to restrictions such as matching the method used for income and expenses.
notes.example: Like a shop that uses accrual for stock purchases and sales but cash for its other income and expenses.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Hybrid method”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: Hybrid method. Generally, you can use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods of accounting if the combination clearly reflects your income and you use it consistently.

notes.front: What is a section 481(a) adjustment?
notes.back: The adjustment ordinarily required when a business changes an accounting method, reported in Part IV of Form 3115.
notes.explanation: The Form 3115 instructions say an adjustment under section 481(a) is ordinarily required for accounting method changes, and they set the period over which it is taken.
notes.example: Like a catch-up entry when a shop switches from cash to accrual: it picks up amounts the old method had not yet counted.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 3115 (Rev. December 2022), “Part IV—Section 481(a) Adjustment”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Part IV-Section 481(a) Adjustment Line 25. Ordinarily, an adjustment under section 481(a) is required for accounting method changes.

notes.front: What is Form 8300, and who must file it?
notes.back: A report of cash payments over $10,000: filed by anyone in a trade or business who receives that much cash in one or related transactions.
notes.explanation: The duty sits with the business receiving the cash, and it covers related transactions as well as single ones.
notes.example: Like a bank’s large-cash report, but made by a car dealer, jeweller or other business that takes the cash.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8300 (Rev. December 2023), “Who must file”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Each person engaged in a trade or business who, in the course of that trade or business, receives more than $10,000 in cash in one transaction or in two or more related transactions, must file Form 8300.

notes.front: What is the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax?
notes.back: A federal unemployment tax paid by employers: for 2025, 6.0% of the first $7,000 of each employee’s wages.
notes.explanation: Pub 15 calls the $7,000 the federal wage base and notes that a state’s wage base may differ.
notes.example: Like a per-employee levy that stops each year once that worker’s pay passes a fixed amount.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Figuring FUTA tax”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: For 2025, the FUTA tax rate is 6.0%. The tax applies to the first $7,000 you pay to each employee as wages during the year. The $7,000 is the federal wage base. Your state wage base may be different.

notes.front: For a Form 941 filer, what is the lookback period?
notes.back: The four quarters, from 1 July to 30 June, whose reported taxes set the employer’s deposit schedule for the calendar year.
notes.explanation: Pub 15 fixes the schedule for the whole calendar year from the taxes reported on Form 941, line 12, in that period.
notes.example: Like a credit score built from last year’s history: past totals decide this year’s deposit rhythm.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Lookback period”, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: your deposit schedule for a calendar year is determined from the total taxes reported on Forms 941, line 12, in a 4-quarter lookback period. The lookback period begins July 1 and ends June 30

notes.front: What is the trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP)?
notes.back: A penalty of 100% of unpaid trust fund taxes (withheld income, social security and Medicare taxes) not withheld, deposited or paid.
notes.explanation: Pub 15 calls these trust fund taxes because they are the taxes that must be withheld from employees.
notes.example: Like being personally charged for money you held in trust for someone else and did not hand over.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Trust fund recovery penalty”, PDF p. 35
notes.evidence: If federal income, social security, or Medicare taxes that must be withheld (that is, trust fund taxes) aren't withheld or aren't deposited or paid to the U.S. Treasury, the trust fund recovery penalty may apply. The penalty is 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax.

notes.front: What three rules must an employer’s reimbursement arrangement meet to be an accountable plan?
notes.back: Expenses have a business connection; the employee adequately accounts for them in a reasonable time; any excess is returned in a reasonable time.
notes.explanation: Pub 463 requires all three rules; an arrangement that misses any of them is not accountable.
notes.example: Like a petty-cash float: you hand in receipts and return the change.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Accountable Plans”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: 1. Your expenses must have a business connection-that is, you must have paid or incurred deductible expenses while performing services as an employee of your employer. 2. You must adequately account to your employer for these expenses within a reasonable period of time. 3. You must return any excess reimbursement or allowance within a reasonable period of time.

notes.front: What is a nonaccountable plan?
notes.back: A reimbursement or expense allowance arrangement that fails one or more of the three accountable plan rules.
notes.explanation: Pub 463 defines it by exclusion: missing any one rule is enough.
notes.example: Like a flat monthly car allowance paid with no mileage records and nothing ever returned.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Nonaccountable Plans”, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: A nonaccountable plan is a reimbursement or expense allowance arrangement that doesn't meet one or more of the three rules listed earlier under Accountable Plans.

notes.front: Under the general rule in Pub 15-A, when is an individual an independent contractor?
notes.back: When the payer can control or direct only the result of the work, not the means and methods of achieving it.
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A adds that whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor depends on the facts in each case.
notes.example: Like hiring a decorator to paint a room by Friday: you judge the finished walls, not how the brushwork is done.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Independent Contractors”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: However, whether such people are employees or independent contractors depends on the facts in each case. The general rule is that an individual is an independent contractor if you, the person for whom the services are performed, have the right to control or direct only the result of the work and not the means and methods of accomplishing the result.

notes.front: What is an applicable large employer (ALE)?
notes.back: For a calendar year, an employer (or aggregated group) that averaged at least 50 full-time employees, including full-time equivalents, in the preceding year.
notes.explanation: The test looks back to the preceding calendar year, so this year’s status depends on last year’s workforce.
notes.example: Like a threshold at a car park barrier: 50 full-time staff last year lifts the employer into the health-coverage reporting rules this year.
notes.source: Instructions for Forms 1094-C and 1095-C (2025), “Definitions: Applicable Large Employer (ALE)”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: An ALE is, for a particular calendar year, any single employer, or group of employers treated as an Aggregated ALE Group, that employed an average of at least 50 full-time employees (including full-time equivalent employees) on business days during the preceding calendar year.

notes.front: A corporation earns 65% of its total receipts from repairing cars and 35% from selling parts. Which activity sets its business activity code on Form 1120?
notes.back: Car repair: the activity producing the highest percentage of total receipts.
notes.choices:
A) Car repair
B) Parts sales
C) Both, with two codes entered
notes.choicesExplained: B: parts sales produce the smaller share of receipts. C: the return asks for the one principal activity, found by the highest share of total receipts.
notes.explanation: The instructions pick the activity from which the corporation derives the highest percentage of its total receipts: 65% beats 35%.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule K, Question 2”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: from which activity the corporation derives the highest percentage of its total receipts.

notes.front: How does a balance sheet differ from an income statement in what it covers?
notes.back: A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity on a given date; an income statement covers income and expenses over a period.
notes.explanation: One is a snapshot at a point in time; the other measures activity across a span of time.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Prepare your financial statements”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: An income statement shows the income and expenses of the business for a given period of time. • A balance sheet shows the assets, liabilities, and your equity in the business on a given date.

notes.front: A corporation need not complete Schedules L, M-1 and M-2 if its total receipts and its year-end total assets are both less than {{c1::$250,000}} and it answers Yes to Schedule K, question 13.
notes.explanation: Both amounts must be under the limit, and the Yes box on question 13 must be checked, for the relief to apply.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule L. Balance Sheets per Books”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: Corporations with total receipts (page 1, line 1a plus lines 4 through 10) and total assets at the end of the tax year less than $250,000 are not required to complete Schedules L, M-1, and M-2 if the "Yes" box on Schedule K, question 13, is checked.

notes.front: A corporation has total receipts of $240,000 and year-end total assets of $262,000. Must it complete Schedule L?
notes.back: Yes. Receipts of $240,000 are under $250,000, but assets of $262,000 are not, so the exemption fails.
notes.choices:
A) No, because receipts are under $250,000
B) Yes, because assets are not under $250,000
C) No, because the two amounts average under $250,000
notes.choicesExplained: A: receipts alone are not enough; assets must also be under $250,000. C: the test is applied to each amount, not to an average.
notes.explanation: Step 1: receipts $240,000 < $250,000. Step 2: assets $262,000 ≥ $250,000. Both must be below the limit, so Schedules L, M-1 and M-2 are required.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule L. Balance Sheets per Books”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: Corporations with total receipts (page 1, line 1a plus lines 4 through 10) and total assets at the end of the tax year less than $250,000 are not required to complete Schedules L, M-1, and M-2

notes.front: A preparer builds Schedule L from tax depreciation figures that differ from the depreciation in the company’s ledger. What is wrong?
notes.back: Schedule L should agree with the corporation’s books and records, so it should use the book figures.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: Schedule L always uses tax figures
B) Schedule L should agree with the books and records
C) Schedule L is optional for every corporation
notes.choicesExplained: A: Schedule L is the balance sheet per books, not per return. C: only corporations meeting the $250,000 test with a Yes on question 13 may skip it.
notes.explanation: Schedule L is titled Balance Sheets per Books, and the instructions say it should agree with the books and records.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule L. Balance Sheets per Books”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: The balance sheets should agree with the corporation's books and records.

notes.front: A corporation with total assets of {{c1::$10 million}} or more on the last day of the tax year must file Schedule M-3 instead of Schedule M-1.
notes.back: $10 million.
notes.explanation: The asset test is measured on the last day of the tax year, on a non-consolidated or consolidated basis as the case may be.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule M-1”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Corporations with total assets non-consolidated (or consolidated for all corporations included within the consolidated tax group) of $10 million or more on the last day of the tax year must file Schedule M-3 (Form 1120) instead of Schedule M-1.

notes.front: At year end a corporation’s Schedule L shows total assets of $9.4 million; the next year they are $10.2 million. Which reconciliation schedule is required in each year?
notes.back: Year 1: Schedule M-1 (M-3 optional). Year 2: Schedule M-3, because assets reached $10 million.
notes.choices:
A) M-1 in year 1, M-3 in year 2
B) M-3 in both years
C) M-1 in both years
notes.choicesExplained: B: at $9.4 million the corporation is below the threshold, so M-3 is only voluntary. C: at $10.2 million it must file M-3 instead of M-1.
notes.explanation: The test is total assets of $10 million or more on Schedule L at year end: $9.4 million is below it, $10.2 million is above it.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule M-3 (Form 1120) (Rev. June 2025), “Who Must File”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: A corporation filing a non-consolidated Form 1120 that reports on Schedule L total assets that equal or exceed $10 million must complete and file Schedule M-3

notes.front: A corporation’s book income is $400,000 after deducting $9,000 of meals, of which $4,500 is not deductible under section 274(n). Where does the $4,500 go on Schedule M-1?
notes.back: Line 5c, with other expenses recorded on the books but not deducted on the return.
notes.choices:
A) Line 5c
B) Line 7
C) Nowhere: meals do not affect the reconciliation
notes.choicesExplained: B: line 7 is for tax-exempt interest. C: the $4,500 was deducted in the books but not on the return, so it is a reconciling item.
notes.explanation: The instructions list meal expenses not deductible under section 274(n) among the items for line 5c.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule M-1, Line 5c”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Line 5c Include any of the following applicable expenses. • Entertainment expenses not deductible under section 274(a). • Meal expenses not deductible under section 274(n).

notes.front: In total, a partnership’s tax-basis capital accounts for its partners rose from $50,000 to $62,000 during the year. Which Form 1065 schedule shows what caused the $12,000 change?
notes.back: Schedule M-2, the analysis of partners’ capital accounts.
notes.choices:
A) Schedule M-2
B) Schedule L
C) Schedule M-1
notes.choicesExplained: B: Schedule L is the balance sheet at each year end, not the analysis of changes. C: Schedule M-1 reconciles book income with income per return.
notes.explanation: Schedule M-2 shows what caused changes during the year in the partners’ tax-basis capital accounts: $62,000 − $50,000 = $12,000 to explain.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1065 (2025), “Schedule M-2. Analysis of Partners’ Capital Accounts”, PDF p. 63
notes.evidence: Show what caused changes during the tax year in the partners' tax-basis capital accounts.

notes.front: A cash-method plumber is paid in December 2025 with a used van worth $8,000 instead of money. What does she include in 2025 income?
notes.back: $8,000: the fair market value of the property received.
notes.choices:
A) $8,000
B) Nothing until she sells the van
C) Nothing, because no cash changed hands
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: under the cash method, property received counts as income at its fair market value when received.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 says a cash-method taxpayer who receives property or services must include their fair market value in income.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Cash Method”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: If you received property and services, you must include their fair market value (FMV) in income.

notes.front: Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you {{c1::actually pay}} them.
notes.back: Actually pay them.
notes.explanation: The rule mirrors the income side, although expenses paid in advance and costs that must be capitalised are exceptions.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Cash Method: Expenses”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: Under the cash method, generally, you deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them.

notes.front: On 1 October 2025 a cash-method business pays $2,400 for a 12-month insurance policy starting that day. Must it capitalise the payment?
notes.back: No. Under the 12-month rule the benefit does not extend beyond 12 months after it begins, so the $2,400 need not be capitalised.
notes.choices:
A) No: the 12-month rule applies
B) Yes: deduct $600 in 2025 and $1,800 in 2026
C) Yes: capitalise and amortise over 3 years
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the general rule for advance payments, but the 12-month rule lets this benefit be deducted when paid. C: nothing in the policy runs beyond 12 months.
notes.explanation: The policy runs 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026: exactly 12 months after the benefit begins, and it ends before the end of 2026.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Expense paid in advance”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Under the 12-month rule, a taxpayer is not required to capitalize amounts paid to create certain rights or benefits for the taxpayer that do not extend beyond the earlier of the following. • 12 months after the right or benefit begins, or • The end of the tax year after the tax year in which payment is made.

notes.front: Which of these generally cannot use the cash method: a C corporation that fails the gross receipts test, an S corporation, or a partnership whose partners are all individuals?
notes.back: The C corporation that fails the gross receipts test.
notes.choices:
A) The C corporation failing the gross receipts test
B) The S corporation
C) The partnership with only individual partners
notes.choicesExplained: B: S corporations are carved out of the excluded list. C: only a partnership with a C corporation partner is excluded.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 excludes corporations other than S corporations, partnerships with such a corporation as a partner, and tax shelters; a corporation that meets the gross receipts test is excepted.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Excluded Entities”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: The following entities generally cannot use the cash method, including any combination of methods that includes the cash method. (However, see Special rules for farming businesses, later.) • A corporation (other than an S corporation). However, see Exceptions below. • A partnership with a corporation (other than an S corporation) as a partner.

notes.front: A C corporation using the cash method fails the gross receipts test for a year. What must it do?
notes.back: Change to an accrual method from that year, filing Form 3115 to request the change.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 makes the change effective for the very year the test is failed, and routes it through Form 3115.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Gross receipts test”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: A corporation or partnership that fails to meet the gross receipts test for any tax year cannot use the cash method and must change to an accrual method of accounting, effective for the tax year in which the entity fails to meet this test. The entity must file Form 3115 to request the change.

notes.front: An accrual-method taxpayer includes income when the all events test is met: all events fixing the right to receive it have occurred and {{c1::the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy}}.
notes.back: The amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 makes both conditions necessary; a right to income with no reasonably determinable amount does not yet meet the test.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Accrual Method: Income”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: This test is met when all events have occurred which fix your right to receive the income and you can determine the amount with reasonable accuracy.

notes.front: An accrual-method engineering firm finishes a fixed-fee $30,000 job and bills it on 20 December 2025. The client pays on 15 January 2026. When is the $30,000 income?
notes.back: 2025: the right to the fee became fixed and the amount was known when the job was finished and billed.
notes.choices:
A) 2025
B) 2026, when paid
C) Half in each year
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the cash method answer. C: nothing splits the fee; the all events test was met in full in 2025.
notes.explanation: Under the all events test the fee is income when the right to it is fixed and the amount reasonably determinable, which happened in December 2025.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Accrual Method: Income”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Generally, you include an amount in gross income for the tax year in which the all events test is met.

notes.front: An accrual-method, calendar-year firm signs a contract in December 2025 for a contractor to repaint its offices in March 2026, paying in April 2026. When is the cost generally deductible?
notes.back: 2026, when the painting is done: that is when economic performance occurs for services provided to the firm.
notes.choices:
A) 2026
B) 2025, when the contract is signed
C) Only when paid, whatever the method
notes.choicesExplained: B: signing the contract does not provide the services, so economic performance has not occurred. C: payment is the cash method test, not the accrual one.
notes.explanation: For services provided to you, economic performance occurs as the services are provided, and the deduction generally waits for it.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Economic Performance”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: If your expense is for property or services provided to you, or for your use of property, economic performance occurs as the property or services are provided or the property is used.

notes.front: A hardware shop needs an inventory to account for its income and does not qualify for the small business taxpayer exception. Which hybrid combination is allowed?
notes.back: An accrual method for purchases and sales, and generally the cash method for its other income and expenses.
notes.choices:
A) Accrual for purchases and sales, cash for the rest
B) Cash for everything
C) Cash for sales and accrual for purchases
notes.choicesExplained: B: where an inventory is needed, purchases and sales must use accrual. C: the rule requires accrual for both purchases and sales.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 requires accrual for purchases and sales where an inventory is necessary, and generally allows cash for all other items.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Hybrid method”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must use an accrual method for purchases and sales. However, see Exception for Small Business Taxpayers, later. Generally, you can use the cash method for all other items of income and expenses.

notes.front: After filing its first return, what does a business generally need before changing its accounting method?
notes.back: Approval from the Internal Revenue Service.
notes.explanation: Pub 538 ties the need for consent to having already set up the method and filed a first return.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Change in Accounting Method”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Once you have set up your accounting method and filed your first return, generally, you must receive approval from the IRS before you change the method.

notes.front: File Form 3115 to request a change in either an overall accounting method or {{c1::the accounting treatment of any item}}.
notes.back: The accounting treatment of any item.
notes.explanation: Form 3115 covers both kinds of change: the whole method, or how one item is treated.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 3115 (Rev. December 2022), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: File Form 3115 to request a change in either an overall accounting method or the accounting treatment of any item.

notes.front: A cash-method business has never applied the 12-month rule to its prepaid expenses. It now wants to deduct qualifying prepayments under that rule. What does Pub 538 require first?
notes.back: Internal Revenue Service approval, requested as a change in accounting method.
notes.choices:
A) Internal Revenue Service approval through a change in accounting method
B) Nothing: the 12-month rule is automatic
C) An amended return for every open year
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 538 says a taxpayer not already applying the rule must obtain approval first. C: Pub 538 points to its section on changing accounting methods, not to amended returns.
notes.explanation: Starting to use the 12-month rule is treated as needing Internal Revenue Service approval, so the business requests it before applying the rule.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Expense paid in advance”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: If you have not been applying the general rule (an expense paid in advance is deductible only in the year to which it applies) and/or the 12-month rule to the expenses you paid in advance, you must obtain approval from the IRS before using the general rule and/or the 12-month rule.

notes.front: A business changes method with a positive section 481(a) adjustment and is not under examination. Over how many tax years is the adjustment generally taken? And if the adjustment were negative?
notes.back: Positive: generally 4 tax years (year of change and the next 3). Negative: generally 1 tax year, the year of change.
notes.choices:
A) 4 years positive, 1 year negative
B) 1 year for both
C) 2 years positive, 4 years negative
notes.choicesExplained: B: a positive adjustment is generally spread over 4 years. C: 2 years applies to a positive adjustment only for many changes made while under examination.
notes.explanation: The Form 3115 instructions set 1 tax year for a negative and 4 tax years for a positive adjustment, as the general rule.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 3115 (Rev. December 2022), “Part IV—Section 481(a) Adjustment”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: The section 481(a) adjustment period is generally 1 tax year (year of change) for a negative section 481(a) adjustment and 4 tax years

notes.front: Generally, a partnership doesn’t pay tax on its income but {{c1::passes through any profits or losses to its partners}}.
notes.back: Passes through any profits or losses to its partners.
notes.explanation: The partners, not the partnership, then include those items on their own returns.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1065 (2025), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Generally, a partnership doesn't pay tax on its income but passes through any profits or losses to its partners. Partners must include partnership items on their tax or information returns.

notes.front: Box 1 of a partner’s Schedule K-1 shows a $40,000 loss. The partner assumes the whole $40,000 is deductible because the partnership reported it. What is the flaw?
notes.back: The deductible loss may be less than the K-1 amount; the partner must consider and apply any limitations.
notes.choices:
A) The partner must apply the loss limitations
B) None: the K-1 figure is always deductible
C) The partnership should have applied the limits before issuing the K-1
notes.choicesExplained: B: the partner’s instructions warn the claimable amount may be smaller. C: the instructions put that responsibility on the partner.
notes.explanation: The partner’s instructions say applying any limitations is the partner’s responsibility, not the partnership’s.
notes.source: Partner’s Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) (2025), “Purpose of Schedule K-1”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The amount of loss and deduction you may claim on your tax return may be less than the amount reported on Schedule K-1. It's the partner's responsibility to consider and apply any applicable limitations.

notes.front: A partnership pays $3,000 of expenses connected with earning tax-exempt municipal bond interest. How is the $3,000 reported to partners?
notes.back: As nondeductible expenses: Schedule K, line 18c, and Schedule K-1 box 18, code C.
notes.choices:
A) Nondeductible expenses, box 18 code C
B) Ordinary business deduction
C) Not reported at all
notes.choicesExplained: B: expenses of producing tax-exempt income are the instructions’ own example of nondeductible expenses. C: they must still be reported.
notes.explanation: The Form 1065 instructions give expenses connected with the production of tax-exempt income as the example of nondeductible expenses.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1065 (2025), “Nondeductible expenses”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Nondeductible expenses (for example, expenses connected with the production of tax-exempt income).

notes.front: On Form 1120-S, what should Schedule L, line 19 (loans from shareholders) generally reconcile to?
notes.back: The sum of the shareholder loan amounts reported on all the Schedules K-1.
notes.explanation: Each K-1 reports the debt the S corporation owes directly to that shareholder, so together they should match the balance-sheet line.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule K-1, Item G”, PDF p. 27
notes.evidence: Report the amount of debt owed by the S corporation directly to the shareholder as of the beginning and end of the S corporation's tax year. Generally, the amount reported on Schedule L, line 19, Loans from shareholders, should reconcile to the sum of all amounts reported on Schedules K-1.

notes.front: What conditions must be met for an automatic Form 7004 extension to be granted?
notes.back: Complete Form 7004 properly, estimate any tax properly, file it by the return’s due date, and pay any tax due.
notes.explanation: The extension is automatic only if all these steps are taken; filing late or skipping payment defeats it.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 7004 (Rev. December 2025), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The extension will be granted if you complete Form 7004 properly, make a proper estimate of the tax (if applicable), file Form 7004 by the due date of the return for which the extension is requested, and pay any tax that is due.

notes.front: The automatic extension of time to file under Form 7004 is generally {{c1::6 months}}.
notes.back: 6 months.
notes.explanation: The exceptions are certain Form 1041 filers and C corporations with tax years ending 30 June.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 7004 (Rev. December 2025), “Maximum extension period”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The automatic extension period for time to file is generally 6 months. Exceptions apply for certain filers of Form 1041 and for C corporations with tax years ending June 30.

notes.front: A calendar-year C corporation and a calendar-year trust filing Form 1041 each file Form 7004 on time. Which one gets an automatic extension shorter than 6 months?
notes.back: The trust: estates and trusts filing Form 1041 get 5½ months; the C corporation gets the general 6 months.
notes.choices:
A) The trust
B) The C corporation
C) Neither: both get 6 months
notes.choicesExplained: B: the shorter or longer periods for corporations apply only to tax years ending 30 June. C: Form 1041 filers are an exception to the 6-month rule.
notes.explanation: Form 1041 filers other than bankruptcy estates are the named exception with 5½ months; a calendar-year corporation has no 30 June year end.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 7004 (Rev. December 2025), “Maximum extension period”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: An estate (other than a bankruptcy estate) and a trust filing Form 1041 are eligible for an automatic 51/2-month extension of time to file.

notes.front: A corporation files Form 7004 on time but pays its $20,000 balance due two months after the regular due date. Is interest charged?
notes.back: Yes: interest runs on the unpaid tax from the regular due date until paid, even with the extension.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, from the regular due date
B) No, because the extension was granted
C) Only if reasonable cause is not shown
notes.choicesExplained: B: Form 7004 extends the time to file, not to pay. C: interest is charged even where reasonable cause for late payment is shown.
notes.explanation: The Form 7004 instructions say interest is charged even if an extension was granted or reasonable cause shown.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 7004 (Rev. December 2025), “Interest”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Interest is charged on any tax not paid by the regular due date of the return from the due date until the tax is paid. It will be charged even if you have been granted an extension or have shown reasonable cause for not paying on time.

notes.front: A business files 12 required information returns for 2025 correctly but 20 days after the due date. What is the penalty before any maximum?
notes.back: 12 × $60 = $720, because each return was correctly filed within 30 days after the due date.
notes.choicesExplained: B: $130 a return applies only when filed more than 30 days late but by 1 August. C: $340 a return applies after 1 August or when not filed.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 20 days late falls in the within-30-days tier, $60 a return. Step 2: 12 × $60 = $720.
notes.source: General Instructions for Certain Information Returns (2025), “Failure To File Correct Information Returns by the Due Date”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: $60 per information return if you correctly file within 30 days after the due date; maximum penalty $683,000 per year ($239,000 for small businesses, defined below).

notes.front: What is the penalty when a failure to file a correct information return is due to intentional disregard?
notes.back: At least $680 per information return, with no maximum.
notes.explanation: Unlike the ordinary tiers, this penalty has no annual maximum.
notes.source: General Instructions for Certain Information Returns (2025), “Intentional disregard of filing requirements”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: If any failure to file a correct information return is due to intentional disregard of the filing or correct information requirements, the penalty is at least $680 per information return with no maximum penalty.

notes.front: A U.S. corporation is 30% owned by a foreign person and bought services from that owner’s foreign affiliate during the year. Which international information return may it need?
notes.back: Form 5472, required generally of a 25% foreign-owned corporation with a reportable transaction with a related party.
notes.choices:
A) Form 5472
B) Form 8300
C) Form 3115
notes.choicesExplained: B: Form 8300 reports large cash receipts. C: Form 3115 requests an accounting method change.
notes.explanation: 30% is at least 25% foreign ownership, and a transaction with a related party brings in the Form 5472 requirement.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Requirement to file Form 5472”, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: Generally, a 25% foreign-owned corporation that had a reportable transaction with a foreign or domestic related party during the tax year must file Form 5472.

notes.front: File Form 8300 by the {{c1::15th}} day after the date the cash was received.
notes.back: The 15th day.
notes.explanation: If that day falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the form is due the next business day.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8300 (Rev. December 2023), “When to file”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: File Form 8300 by the 15th day after the date the cash was received. If that date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, file the form on the next business day.

notes.front: For Form 8300, which transactions count as related?
notes.back: Any between a payer and recipient within 24 hours, and longer series the recipient knows or has reason to know are connected.
notes.explanation: Time alone does not break the link: a longer series still counts if the recipient knows or has reason to know it is connected.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8300 (Rev. December 2023), “Related transactions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Any transactions conducted between a payer (or its agent) and the recipient in a 24-hour period are related transactions. Transactions are considered related even if they occur over a period of more than 24 hours if the recipient knows, or has reason to know, that each transaction is one of a series of connected transactions.

notes.front: A car dealer receives $6,000 in currency from a buyer on Monday afternoon and a further $5,500 in currency the next morning for the same car. Must it file Form 8300, and by when?
notes.back: Yes: $11,500 in related transactions within 24 hours exceeds $10,000; file by the 15th day after receipt.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, by the 15th day after receipt
B) No, because neither payment exceeds $10,000
C) Yes, but only by 31 January next year
notes.choicesExplained: B: related transactions are added together. C: 31 January is the deadline for the statement to the buyer, not the form.
notes.explanation: Step 1: the payments fall within 24 hours, so they are related. Step 2: $6,000 + $5,500 = $11,500, which is more than $10,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8300 (Rev. December 2023), “Related transactions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Any transactions conducted between a payer (or its agent) and the recipient in a 24-hour period are related transactions.

notes.front: For 2025, the social security tax rate is 6.2% each for employer and employee, and the Medicare rate is {{c1::1.45%}} each.
notes.explanation: Each rate applies to both parties, giving totals of 12.4% and 2.9%.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Social security and Medicare taxes”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: For 2025, the social security tax rate is 6.2% (amount withheld) each for the employer and employee (12.4% total). The social security wage base limit is $176,100. The tax rate for Medicare is 1.45% (amount withheld) each for the employee and employer (2.9% total).

notes.front: For 2025, the social security wage base limit is {{c1::$176,100}}; there is no wage base limit for Medicare tax.
notes.explanation: Social security withholding stops once wages reach the base, while Medicare continues on all wages.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “What’s New: Social security and Medicare tax for 2025”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: The social security wage base limit is $176,100. The Medicare tax rate is 1.45% each for the employee and employer, unchanged from 2024. There is no wage base limit for Medicare tax.

notes.front: An employee earns $190,000 in wages in 2025. How much social security and Medicare tax is withheld from the employee?
notes.choicesExplained: B: social security stops at the $176,100 wage base. C: Medicare has no wage base, so it applies to all $190,000.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Social security and Medicare taxes”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: For 2025, the social security tax rate is 6.2% (amount withheld) each for the employer and employee (12.4% total). The social security wage base limit is $176,100.

notes.front: With the maximum 5.4% credit for state unemployment tax, the FUTA tax rate after credit is {{c1::0.6%}}.
notes.explanation: 6.0% less the 5.4% credit leaves 0.6%, for an employer that paid its state unemployment taxes in full, on time and on the same wages.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Figuring FUTA tax”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: The credit may be as much as 5.4% of FUTA taxable wages. If you're entitled to the maximum 5.4% credit, the FUTA tax rate after credit is 0.6%. You're entitled to the maximum credit if you paid your state unemployment taxes in full, on time, and on all the same wages as are subject to FUTA tax

notes.front: An employer pays three employees $30,000, $12,000 and $5,000 in 2025 and qualifies for the full 5.4% credit. What is its FUTA tax?
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is 0.6% of all $47,000; wages above $7,000 per employee are not taxed. C: that is 6.0% before the credit.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Figuring FUTA tax”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: The tax applies to the first $7,000 you pay to each employee as wages during the year.

notes.front: When must an employer deposit FUTA tax for a quarter?
notes.back: If the liability is over $500, by the last day of the month after the quarter; if $500 or less, it may carry it forward.
notes.explanation: Small quarterly amounts roll into the next quarter until the running total passes $500.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “When to deposit (FUTA)”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: If your FUTA tax liability for any calendar quarter is $500 or less, you don't have to deposit the tax. Instead, you may carry it forward and add it to the liability figured in the next quarter to see if you must make a deposit.

notes.front: If an employer reported {{c1::$50,000 or less}} of taxes for the lookback period, it is a monthly schedule depositor; more than that makes it semiweekly.
notes.back: $50,000 or less.
notes.explanation: The deposit schedule for the whole calendar year is fixed by this single test.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Lookback period”, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: If you reported $50,000 or less of taxes for the lookback period, you're a monthly schedule depositor; if you reported more than $50,000, you're a semiweekly schedule depositor.

notes.front: A Form 941 filer reported $11,000, $13,000, $14,000 and $15,000 on line 12 for the quarters from 1 July 2023 to 30 June 2024. What is its deposit schedule for 2025?
notes.back: Semiweekly: the lookback total is $53,000, more than $50,000.
notes.choices:
A) Semiweekly
B) Monthly
C) Quarterly with the return
notes.choicesExplained: B: monthly requires $50,000 or less. C: paying with the return depends on a quarter under $2,500, not on the lookback period.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Lookback period”, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: If you reported $50,000 or less of taxes for the lookback period, you're a monthly schedule depositor; if you reported more than $50,000, you're a semiweekly schedule depositor.

notes.front: By when does a monthly schedule depositor deposit employment taxes on a month’s payments?
notes.back: By the 15th day of the following month.
notes.explanation: Pub 15 sets one deposit a month for these employers, subject to the $100,000 next-day rule.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Monthly Deposit Schedule”, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: Under the monthly deposit schedule, deposit employment taxes on payments made during a month by the 15th day of the following month.

notes.front: Under the semiweekly schedule, by when are taxes on payments made on a Wednesday, Thursday or Friday deposited?
notes.back: By the following Wednesday.
notes.explanation: The semiweekly schedule pairs each group of pay days with a fixed deposit day.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Semiweekly Deposit Schedule”, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: Under the semiweekly deposit schedule, deposit employment taxes for payments made on Wednesday, Thursday, and/or Friday by the following Wednesday.

notes.front: If an employer accumulates {{c1::$100,000}} or more in taxes on any day during a deposit period, it must deposit by the next business day.
notes.explanation: This rule applies whether the employer is a monthly or a semiweekly depositor.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “$100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: If you accumulate $100,000 or more in taxes on any day during a monthly or semiweekly deposit period (see Deposit period, earlier in this section), you must deposit the tax by the next business day, whether you're a monthly or semiweekly schedule depositor.

notes.front: A monthly schedule depositor pays annual bonuses on Tuesday 9 December 2025 and accumulates $104,000 of employment taxes that day. When must it deposit?
notes.back: By Wednesday 10 December 2025, the next business day.
notes.choices:
A) 10 December 2025
B) 15 January 2026
C) 17 December 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B: the monthly due date is overridden once $100,000 accumulates in a day. C: no rule gives 17 December; the next-day rule applies to monthly and semiweekly depositors alike.
notes.explanation: $104,000 is at least $100,000, so the next-day rule applies regardless of the monthly schedule.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “$100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: you must deposit the tax by the next business day, whether you're a monthly or semiweekly schedule depositor.

notes.front: When may a Form 941 filer pay its employment taxes with the return instead of depositing them?
notes.back: When its total tax liability for the quarter (Form 941, line 12) is less than $2,500.
notes.explanation: Pub 15 bases the test on the quarter’s total liability on Form 941, line 12.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Calendar: File Form 941”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: You may pay these taxes with Form 941 if your total tax liability for the quarter (Form 941, line 12) is less than $2,500.

notes.front: How does Form 944 differ from Form 941, and who may file it?
notes.back: Form 944 is annual, Form 941 quarterly. Form 944 needs written Internal Revenue Service notice, for employers expecting $1,000 or less of employment taxes.
notes.explanation: An employer cannot simply switch; it must ask in the first calendar quarter and receive written notice.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “What’s New / Form 944”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: If you've been filing quarterly Forms 941 and believe your employment taxes for the calendar year will be $1,000 or less, and you would like to file an annual Form 944 instead of quarterly Forms 941, you must contact the IRS during the first calendar quarter of the tax year to request to file Form 944.

notes.front: On whom may the trust fund recovery penalty be imposed?
notes.back: On all persons the Internal Revenue Service finds responsible for collecting, accounting for or paying over the taxes who acted willfully in not doing so.
notes.explanation: It reaches individuals when the unpaid taxes cannot be immediately collected from the employer or business.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Trust fund recovery penalty”, PDF p. 35
notes.evidence: If these unpaid taxes can't be immediately collected from the employer or business, the trust fund recovery penalty may be imposed on all persons who are determined by the IRS to be responsible for collecting, accounting for, or paying over these taxes, and who acted willfully in not doing so.

notes.front: A company withheld $6,000 of income tax and $2,295 of employee social security and Medicare tax but paid none of it; its own matching share of $2,295 is also unpaid. What is the maximum TFRP?
notes.back: $8,295: 100% of the withheld taxes ($6,000 + $2,295). The employer’s own share is not a trust fund tax.
notes.choicesExplained: B: that adds the employer’s matching share, which is not withheld from employees. C: that leaves out the withheld employee social security and Medicare tax.
notes.explanation: Trust fund taxes are those that must be withheld. Step 1: $6,000 + $2,295 = $8,295. Step 2: the penalty is 100% of that.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Trust fund recovery penalty”, PDF p. 35
notes.evidence: If federal income, social security, or Medicare taxes that must be withheld (that is, trust fund taxes) aren't withheld or aren't deposited or paid to the U.S. Treasury, the trust fund recovery penalty may apply. The penalty is 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax.

notes.front: The quarterly excise tax return, Form 720, for January to March is due by {{c1::30 April}}.
notes.back: 30 April.
notes.explanation: The due date falls at the end of the month after the quarter closes.
notes.source: Publication 510 (Rev. December 2025), Excise Taxes, “Due dates”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: Form 720 must be filed by the following due dates. Quarter Covered Due Dates January, February, March . . . . . April 30

notes.front: Generally, how long must a business keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return?
notes.back: Until the period of limitations for that return runs out.
notes.explanation: The limitations period is the time in which the taxpayer can amend or the Internal Revenue Service can assess, so the records must last as long.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “How Long To Keep Records”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out. The period of limitations is the period of time in which you can amend your return to claim a credit or refund, or the IRS can assess additional tax.

notes.front: If a business does not report income it should and the omission is more than 25% of the gross income shown on the return, the period of limitations is {{c1::6 years}}.
notes.back: 6 years.
notes.explanation: The longer period turns on the size of the omission: more than 25% of the gross income shown on the return.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Table 3. Period of Limitations”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Do not report income that you should report and it is more than 25% of the gross income shown on the return 6 years

notes.front: An employer must keep all employment tax records for at least {{c1::4 years}} after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.
notes.back: 4 years.
notes.explanation: Employment tax records have their own minimum, measured from the later of the due date or payment date.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Employment taxes”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.

notes.front: A client bought a machine in 2016, depreciated it, and sold it in 2025. She asks whether she can now shred the 2016 purchase records. What do you advise?
notes.back: Keep them until the period of limitations expires for 2025, the year of the taxable disposition.
notes.choices:
A) Keep them until the limitations period for 2025 expires
B) Shred them: the 2016 return is closed
C) Keep them for 4 years from purchase
notes.choicesExplained: B: property records are measured from the year of disposition, not purchase. C: 4 years is the employment tax record rule.
notes.explanation: The purchase records prove basis and depreciation, which are needed to figure the gain or loss on the 2025 sale.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Assets”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. You must keep these records to figure any depreciation, amortization, or depletion deduction, and to figure your basis for computing gain or loss

notes.front: A self-employed surveyor records each week’s business mileage every Friday in a logbook. Her partner rebuilds his log from memory in December. Whose log is more likely to be treated as timely kept?
notes.back: Hers: a log kept weekly counts as a timely kept record; one prepared much later lacks accurate recall.
notes.choices:
A) Hers, kept weekly
B) His, because it covers the whole year
C) Neither: entries must be made on the day of each trip
notes.choicesExplained: B: a statement prepared later has less value because of poor recall. C: Pub 463 says the elements need not be written down on the day.
notes.explanation: Pub 463 says a log maintained on a weekly basis that accounts for use during the week is considered a timely kept record.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Timely kept records”, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: If you maintain a log on a weekly basis that accounts for use during the week, the log is considered a timely kept record.

notes.front: An employee gets a $1,500 travel advance under her employer’s accountable plan, accounts for $1,200 of expenses within 30 days, and returns $300 within 60 days. What goes in box 1 of her Form W-2?
notes.back: Nothing: she met all three accountable plan rules, so none of the $1,500 is included in her wages.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) $300
C) $1,500
notes.choicesExplained: B: the $300 excess was returned within a reasonable period. C: amounts paid under an accountable plan that meets the rules are not wages.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $1,500 − $1,200 accounted for = $300 excess. Step 2: she accounted and returned the excess in time, meeting all three rules, so the employer should not include the reimbursement in box 1.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Employee meets accountable plan rules”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: If you meet the three rules for accountable plans, your employer shouldn't include any reimbursements in your income in box 1 of your Form W-2.

notes.front: An employer pays a salesman a flat $400 a month car allowance with no mileage records required and nothing returned. How is the $4,800 for the year treated?
notes.back: As wages under a nonaccountable plan: included in box 1 of his Form W-2.
notes.choices:
A) Wages in box 1 of Form W-2
B) Tax-free reimbursement
C) Tax-free if he later hands in a mileage log
notes.choicesExplained: B: the plan fails the accounting and return rules. C: the plan itself never required accounting or the return of any excess, so it is nonaccountable.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $400 × 12 = $4,800. Step 2: with no accounting and no return of excess, the plan is nonaccountable and the employer reports the total as wages.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Reimbursement of Nondeductible Expenses”, PDF p. 47
notes.evidence: under a nonaccountable plan with your wages, salary, or other pay. Your employer will report the total in box 1 of your Form W-2.

notes.front: In a sole proprietorship, whose are the business’s liabilities?
notes.back: The owner’s: the business has no existence apart from the owner, so its liabilities are the owner’s personal liabilities.
notes.explanation: Pub 583 calls it the simplest form to start and maintain, but the owner bears the risks with all assets.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Sole proprietorships”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: It is the simplest form of business organization to start and maintain. The business has no existence apart from you, the owner. Its liabilities are your personal liabilities.

notes.front: The profit of a C corporation is taxed to the corporation when earned and then taxed to the shareholders {{c1::when distributed as dividends}}.
notes.back: When distributed as dividends.
notes.explanation: Shareholders also cannot deduct the corporation’s losses, which Pub 583 notes alongside the two layers of tax.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “C corporations”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The profit of a C corporation is taxed to the corporation when earned, and then is taxed to the shareholders when distributed as dividends. However, shareholders cannot deduct any loss of the corporation.

notes.front: Two founders of an eligible domestic corporation want profits taxed once, to them, rather than to the corporation and again as dividends. What does Pub 583 point to?
notes.back: Electing S corporation status, which avoids double taxation if the corporation meets the tests.
notes.choices:
A) Elect S corporation status
B) Stay a C corporation and pay no dividends
C) Nothing can avoid the two layers of tax
notes.choicesExplained: B: the corporation would still pay tax on its profit when earned. C: Pub 583 says an eligible corporation can avoid double taxation by electing S status.
notes.explanation: Pub 583 says an eligible corporation avoids tax once to the corporation and again to the shareholders by meeting certain tests and electing S status.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “S corporations”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: An eligible domestic corporation (or a domestic entity eligible to elect to be treated as a corporation) can avoid double taxation (once to the corporation and again to the shareholders) as long as it meets certain tests and elects to be treated as an S corporation.

notes.front: A client forms a limited liability company under state law. For federal income tax, how may it be classified?
notes.back: As a partnership, a corporation, or an entity disregarded as separate from its owner.
notes.choices:
A) Partnership, corporation or disregarded entity
B) Always a corporation
C) Always a sole proprietorship
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: Pub 583 says a limited liability company may take any of three classifications under the entity rules.
notes.explanation: Its members are not personally liable for its debts, but its tax classification is set separately by the classification rules.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Limited liability company”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The members of an LLC are not personally liable for its debts. An LLC may be classified for federal income tax purposes as either a partnership, a corporation, or an entity disregarded as separate from its owner

notes.front: What does Pub 583 advise about a business bank account when starting out?
notes.back: Open a business checking account and keep it separate from the personal account.
notes.explanation: Pub 583 calls the business checkbook the basic source for recording business expenses, so daily receipts should go into it.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Business checkbook”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: One of the first things you should do when you start a business is open a business checking account. You should keep your business account separate from your personal checking account. The business checkbook is your basic source of information for recording your business expenses.

notes.front: A calendar-year corporation dissolves on 10 August 2025. By when must it generally file its final Form 1120?
notes.back: 15 December 2025: the 15th day of the 4th month after dissolution.
notes.choices:
A) 15 December 2025
B) 15 April 2026
C) 10 November 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the normal calendar-year date, but a dissolved corporation files by reference to its dissolution date. C: the rule is the 15th day of the 4th month.
notes.explanation: Count 4 months after August: September, October, November, December; then the 15th day, giving 15 December.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: A corporation that has dissolved must generally file by the 15th day of the 4th month after the date it dissolved.

notes.front: Under common-law rules, when is a worker generally an employee?
notes.back: When the payer has the right to control what will be done and how it will be done.
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A says it is the right to control the details that matters, even if the employee is given freedom of action.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Common-Law Employees”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Under common-law rules, anyone who performs services for you is generally your employee if you have the right to control what will be done and how it will be done. This is so even when you give the employee freedom of action. What matters is that you have the right to control the details of how the services are performed.

notes.front: In worker classification, which category of evidence covers the instructions a business gives about when, where and how to work?
notes.back: Behavioural control.
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A describes it as facts showing whether the business can direct and control how the worker does the task.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Behavioral control”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Behavioral control. Facts that show whether the business has a right to direct and control how the worker does the task for which the worker is hired

notes.front: In worker classification, which category of evidence covers unreimbursed business expenses and fixed ongoing costs?
notes.back: Financial control.
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A says independent contractors are more likely than employees to have unreimbursed expenses.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Financial control”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Financial control. Facts that show whether the business has a right to control the business aspects of the worker's job include the following. The extent to which the worker has unreimbursed business expenses. Independent contractors are more likely to have unreimbursed expenses than are employees.

notes.front: In worker classification, which category of evidence covers written contracts, employee-type benefits and the permanency of the relationship?
notes.back: Type of relationship (of the parties).
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A lists these facts as showing the relationship the parties intended and actually have.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Type of relationship”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Type of relationship. Facts that show the parties' type of relationship include the following. • Written contracts describing the relationship the parties intended to create.

notes.front: A bakery hires a web designer to deliver a finished website by June for a fixed fee. The bakery reviews only the result; the designer uses her own software and sets her own hours. How is she generally classified?
notes.back: As an independent contractor: the bakery controls only the result, not the means and methods.
notes.choices:
A) Independent contractor
B) Common-law employee
C) Statutory employee
notes.choicesExplained: B: the bakery has no right to control how the work is done. C: web design is not among the statutory employee categories in Pub 15-A.
notes.explanation: The general rule makes a worker an independent contractor where the payer controls only the result of the work.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Independent Contractors”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: an individual is an independent contractor if you, the person for whom the services are performed, have the right to control or direct only the result of the work and not the means and methods of accomplishing the result.

notes.front: A firm tells a bookkeeper which hours to work, which software to use and how to post entries, and gives her paid holiday and a pension. Which is she?
notes.back: A common-law employee: the firm controls how the work is done, and the benefits point the same way.
notes.choices:
A) Common-law employee
B) Independent contractor
C) Either, at the firm’s choice
notes.choicesExplained: B: control over the means and methods marks an employee. C: status turns on the facts, not the label the firm prefers.
notes.explanation: Instructions on when, where and how show behavioural control, and employee-type benefits show the type of relationship.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Behavioral control”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: An employee is generally subject to the business' instructions about when, where, and how to work.

notes.front: What can a business file to have the Internal Revenue Service decide whether a worker is an employee?
notes.back: Form SS-8.
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A points to Form SS-8 when the business wants an Internal Revenue Service determination rather than its own.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “IRS help”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: If you want the IRS to determine whether or not a worker is an employee, file Form SS-8 with the IRS.

notes.front: A full-time city salesperson, independent under the common-law rules, turns in orders to a firm from restaurants for supplies they use in their business. Which statutory category may she fall into?
notes.back: Statutory employee: a full-time traveling or city salesperson taking orders for supplies used in the buyer’s business.
notes.choices:
A) Statutory employee
B) Common-law employee
C) Household employee
notes.choicesExplained: B: the facts say she is independent under the common-law rules. C: she works in a business setting, not a private home.
notes.explanation: Pub 15-A treats such salespeople as employees by statute for certain employment tax purposes if the other conditions are met.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Statutory Employees”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: A full-time traveling or city salesperson who works on your behalf and turns in orders to you from wholesalers; retailers; contractors; or operators of hotels, restaurants, or other similar establishments.

notes.front: A client bought qualified equipment for $80,000 in March 2025 and placed it in service that month. She makes no section 179 election and does not elect out. What special depreciation allowance may she claim?
notes.back: $80,000: 100% × $80,000, since she acquired and placed it in service after 19 January 2025.
notes.choices:
A) $80,000
B) $32,000
C) Nothing: only section 179 gives first-year relief
notes.choicesExplained: B: 40% × $80,000 applies to property acquired before 20 January 2025. C: the special allowance applies unless she elects out.
notes.explanation: Step 1: acquired and placed in service in March 2025, after 19 January 2025, so the 100% rate applies. Step 2: 100% × $80,000 = $80,000.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: reinstated the 100% special depreciation allowance for certain qualified property acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025

notes.front: A client with a loss year would rather spread depreciation on this year’s 5-year property over the recovery period. Can he decline the special depreciation allowance?
notes.back: Yes: he can elect out for a whole class of property, covering all property in that class placed in service that year.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, class by class
B) No, it is mandatory
C) Yes, but only asset by asset
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 946 provides an election not to claim it. C: the election is made for a whole class, not a single asset.
notes.explanation: Pub 946 frames the election by class of property, covering all property in that class placed in service during the year.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “How Can You Elect Not To Claim an Allowance?”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: You can elect, for any class of property, not to deduct any special depreciation allowances for all property in such class placed in service during the tax year.

notes.front: In 2024 an employer averaged 44 full-time employees and 9 full-time equivalent employees on business days. Is it an applicable large employer for 2025?
notes.back: Yes: 44 + 9 = 53, at least 50 full-time employees including equivalents in the preceding year.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, because full-time employees alone are under 50
C) Only if it had 50 employees in 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B: full-time equivalent employees count towards the 50. C: the test uses the preceding calendar year.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 44 full-time + 9 equivalents = 53. Step 2: 53 ≥ 50 in 2024, so it is an ALE for 2025.
notes.source: Instructions for Forms 1094-C and 1095-C (2025), “Definitions: Applicable Large Employer (ALE)”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: employed an average of at least 50 full-time employees (including full-time equivalent employees) on business days during the preceding calendar year.

notes.front: An ALE Member had 120 employees in 2025, of whom 70 were full-time for at least one month. For how many must it file Form 1095-C?
notes.back: At least the 70 employees who were full-time for any month of the year.
notes.choices:
A) The 70 full-time employees
B) All 120 employees are required
C) None unless it offered coverage
notes.choicesExplained: B: the requirement is for full-time employees, though an employer may choose to file for others. C: the form is required for full-time employees whether or not coverage was offered.
notes.explanation: The instructions require a Form 1095-C for each employee who was full-time for any month of the calendar year.
notes.source: Instructions for Forms 1094-C and 1095-C (2025), “Who Must File”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: must file a Form 1095-C for each employee who was a full-time employee of the ALE Member for any month of the calendar year.

notes.front: For calendar year 2025, by when must Forms 1094-C and 1095-C be filed with the Internal Revenue Service?
notes.back: By 2 March 2026 on paper, or 31 March 2026 if filed electronically.
notes.explanation: Filing electronically gives an employer four more weeks than filing on paper.
notes.source: Instructions for Forms 1094-C and 1095-C (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: For calendar year 2025, Forms 1094-C and 1095-C are required to be filed by March 2, 2026, or March 31, 2026, if filing electronically.
